'You've been rubbing your eyes since nine,' said Tejas, sliding into the seat across from Vaibhav in the canteen. 'And you snapped at the intern over a typo.'
'I know.' Vaibhav stirred the tea without drinking it. 'I've been tired every day for weeks, even after a Sunday lie-in. And last night around eight I got that dread in my stomach about Monday. Third Sunday running.'
'Maybe you just need a rest weekend.'
'I thought that too. But I've had rest weekends. The tiredness is back by Tuesday. That's not one bad week. It's a pattern.'
'So?'
'So I'm not going to push through it. Something in how I work has to change. I'll talk to my manager about the team's load, and I'll see a doctor if it doesn't lift.'
Tejas nodded slowly. 'Good. I'll take the Thursday review off your list.'

passage:
The Sunday it clicked, I was lying on the sofa at nine and my stomach was already knotting about Monday's stand-up. I made myself list what I'd been noticing. Tired even after eight hours' sleep. Snapping at Nilesh over a typo in a report that didn't matter; he just said, "Sorry, Kishore," and looked at the floor. The same dread every Sunday for, I counted back, eleven weeks.
My first thought was, "I just need a proper weekend off." But I'd had one in October, and the dread was back the very next Sunday. So rest alone wasn't the fix. Something in how I was working was producing this, week after week.
That was uncomfortable to admit. I'm the team lead; I'm supposed to be the steady one. But I wrote it down: this is a pattern, not a bad week. Then I booked time with my own manager for Tuesday.

qa.q: For how many weeks had the Sunday dread been coming?
qa.a: The same dread had come every Sunday for eleven weeks.

qa.q: Why was it uncomfortable for Kishore to admit it was a pattern?
qa.a: Kishore felt ashamed and a bit afraid, because as team lead Kishore expected to be the steady one.

qa.q: What could Kishore raise with the manager on Tuesday?
qa.a: Kishore could look for the root cause, such as workload or meeting load, and ask about delegating some tasks rather than only taking time off.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have experienced Kishore before this?
qa.a: Nilesh was snapped at over a small typo, so Nilesh may have felt confused or hurt by a lead who seemed irritable for no clear reason.

grounding: It shows a team lead reasoning through fatigue, irritability and Sunday dread and concluding it is a pattern that needs a change, not just a rest weekend.

Manager's note, 3 March.
Pema has led the support team for two years and rarely complains. In our one-to-one today he began by saying he was fine, then stopped. He listed things he had noticed: waking up tired, getting short with his team in the afternoons, and a heavy feeling every Sunday evening before the week began. He said he had taken a long weekend in January hoping it would reset him, and it hadn't. "It keeps coming back, so it's not about one weekend. Something in the way I'm running things has to change," he said.
I thanked him for raising it early. We agreed he would see the office counsellor this week, and I will take two of his recurring meetings off him from Monday. We will review in three weeks.
— Harish

qa.q: What did Pema say about the long weekend in January?
qa.a: He had taken it hoping it would reset him, and it hadn't.

qa.q: What might Pema have been feeling when he said he was fine, then stopped?
qa.a: Pema was likely hesitant and a little embarrassed to admit the strain, but also relieved to finally name the pattern.

qa.q: Which other approach could work alongside dropping two meetings?
qa.a: Pema could look for the root cause of the Sunday dread, such as which tasks drain him most, and delegate some of them.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Harish?
qa.a: Harish sees an early warning worth acting on and responds with concrete support: the counsellor visit, two fewer meetings and a review in three weeks.

grounding: It shows a team lead noticing tiredness, irritability and Sunday dread and concluding that a lasting change is needed rather than another rest weekend.
